summary:
VitalOrbit is a web-based crew health monitor for long-duration space missions, demonstrated with a fictional Expedition Meridian-7 crew. Astronauts log daily check-ins covering vital signs, sleep, body mass, radiation dose, exercise, reaction time, mood, stress, isolation and symptoms. VitalOrbit compares these with each person’s own baseline and rates six areas — cardiovascular and fluid shift, immune, bone and muscle, behavioral health, sleep and circadian rhythm, and radiation — as Nominal, Watch or Action needed, then offers clear protocols and emergency procedures.

This lets astronauts evaluate and act on their own health status, supported by trend charts, a health diary, a simulated ECG, two-tap crew and medical alerts that sync live across devices, and server-enforced privacy: crew see only their own data, while the Commander has read-only oversight.

This matters because on long missions, astronauts must spot health changes in themselves while far from Earth. Early, clear and actionable feedback on radiation, bone, immune and behavioral changes supports faster decisions and crew safety.

VitalOrbit is an unofficial educational demo: all data is simulated and thresholds are illustrative, not clinically validated.
details:
VitalOrbit is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions watch their own health and decide what to do about it. It is demonstrated with a fictional crew on Expedition Meridian-7: Commander, Crew Medical Officer, Pilot, Flight Engineer and Mission Specialist.

Collecting data. Each crew member logs a daily check-in covering:

heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂ and temperature

sleep, body mass, exercise and radiation dose

mood, stress, isolation and symptoms

reaction time, taken from a built-in reaction test

Evaluating health. Rule-based logic compares each entry with that person’s own earlier readings, because “normal” differs between people. It rates six areas as Nominal, Watch or Action needed:

cardiovascular and fluid shift

immune and infection

bone and muscle

behavioral health and cognition

sleep and circadian rhythm

radiation exposure

Acting on it. Every concern links to a protocol with concrete steps. The app also provides:

trend charts and a personal diary

emergency procedures for fire, depressurization, toxic atmosphere, radiation storm and medical emergency

a two-tap alert to the whole crew or to the Crew Medical Officer

Mission features.

crew readiness overview and vehicle-system status

a radiation-storm simulation

individual and team objectives

optional side missions that the Commander creates and crew accept

a simulated ECG at the latest heart rate

a cabin sound monitor that reacts to the microphone or an audio file

How the hosted version works. A Node.js server stores the data, enforces who can see what, and pushes alerts live to every signed-in device.

Crew members receive only their own health data.

The Commander can open anyone’s data, read-only.

Everyone sees only crew readiness counts.

A whole-crew alert shows a banner and sounds a siren on every device in that room. A medical alert is visible only to the sender, the Commander and the Crew Medical Officer, and has no siren.

In the public demo, each visitor gets a private demo crew with a room code that others can use to join.

What benefits does it have?

Self-monitoring when Earth is far away. Astronauts get clear, personal feedback even when contact with ground support is delayed.

Early warning. Comparing each person with their own trend can catch slow changes, such as sleep loss, rising dose or falling mood, before they become acute.

Clear next steps. Every status leads to an action, not just a number.

Privacy with oversight. Leadership sees readiness without crew members seeing each other’s health data.

Reliable emergencies. Two-tap confirmation prevents accidental alarms, and alerts reach the right people at once, with a visual banner and a screen-reader announcement as well as sound.

Open to everyone. Anyone can try it in a browser, with no install and no account.

What is the intended impact?

The project aims to show how a crew on missions to the Moon and Mars could be better aware of, and quicker to act on, their own health. It focuses on radiation, isolation, altered gravity, immune changes and behavioral health. It also works as a teaching and showcase tool that lets students and the public see how spaceflight affects the body. It is an unofficial educational demo, not a medical device.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with no front-end framework. The server is Node.js.

Front end:

SVG for trend charts.

Canvas for the ECG, audio visualizer, particles and meteors.

Web Audio API for synthesized sounds and audio analysis.

Web Animations API and CSS transitions for animation.

Back end: Express for the JSON API, and Server-Sent Events for live updates.

Security: scrypt-hashed passcodes, signed HttpOnly session cookies, a Content-Security-Policy, rate limiting and server-side input checks.

Deployment and testing: Docker, a README with hosting steps, and Playwright browser tests.

AI assistance: Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped write and test the code. Adjust this line to your event’s disclosure rules.

Hardware: None is required. It runs in any modern browser, and a microphone is optional for the sound monitor.

How is your project creative?

Personal baselines: Each astronaut is compared with themselves rather than a population average.

Sound design: Clicks, typing and tab changes sound like a mechanical keyboard, with a chime for success. A siren is reserved for whole-crew emergencies, so routine use never causes alarm fatigue.

Mission-control motion: Animation is precise and never bouncy. The nav indicator glides between tabs, charts draw themselves on, new readings appear as new points, and dropdowns fade, slide and stagger their items with an animated checkmark.

Atmosphere: Interactive particles react to the pointer, clicks and scrolling and recover quickly. Meteors cross the screen, and the particles pulse with audio level.

Live ECG and sound monitor: A synthetic ECG draws in and sweeps at the latest heart rate, and the cabin sound monitor responds to real microphone or file input.

Demo design: Private demo rooms with shareable codes let a showcase audience try it without disturbing each other.

Original identity: It has its own name, terminology, logo and design language.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty and safety: Simulated readings are labeled as simulated, thresholds are called illustrative and not clinically validated, and an on-screen notice says it is an unofficial demo.

Privacy: Health data is the most sensitive, so the server enforces access instead of just hiding things in the interface. The Commander’s access is read-only, and emergency banners no longer reveal the sender’s health status.

Emergency reliability: Confirmation before sending, live delivery to every device, and non-sound backups for each alert: a banner, a screen-reader announcement and a vibration cue on phones.

Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, skip link, labeled charts, screen-reader support, and dropdowns that follow the standard listbox pattern. Reduced-motion users get effects off by default, and sound, effects and theme can each be switched off.

Cognitive load: A minimal, high-contrast interface, because crew are often tired and stressed.

Independence: No agency logos, flags, branding or mission identifiers. A separate file lists the replaced names.

Safe public hosting: Isolated demo rooms, caps on how many exist, per-network limits, and no personal data collected.

Performance: The particle count scales to the screen, effects pause when the tab is hidden, and the blur effect behind menus is light enough for most devices.
